title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
description: Grade 11 Biology: the cell cycle and its phases, mitosis (karyokinesis and cytokinesis) and its significance, and meiosis with crossing over and genetic recombination.

topics.title: The Cell Cycle and Its Phases
topics.concept:
Cells reproduce by dividing into two. The orderly sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its contents and divides into two daughter cells is called the cell cycle. In a typical human cell the cycle takes about 24 hours and has two broad stages: a long preparation stage called interphase and a short dividing stage called the M phase (mitotic phase).

Interphase is often called the resting phase, but the cell is actually very active — it grows and copies its DNA in readiness for division. It is divided into three parts:

  • G1 phase (Gap 1) — the cell grows in size and is metabolically active; the DNA is not yet copied.
  • S phase (Synthesis) — the DNA replicates, so the amount of DNA doubles. (The chromosome number stays the same; each chromosome now has two sister chromatids.)
  • G2 phase (Gap 2) — the cell continues to grow and makes proteins, getting ready to divide.

After G2, the cell enters the M phase, in which the nucleus divides (karyokinesis) followed by the cytoplasm (cytokinesis). Some cells that no longer divide (like mature nerve cells) leave the cycle and enter an inactive stage called G0 (quiescent stage).

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the two broad stages of the cell cycle.
examples.solution:
The cycle has a long and a short stage.

  • Interphase (the long preparation stage).
  • M phase / mitotic phase (the short division stage).
examples.answer: Interphase and the M phase (mitotic phase).

examples.problem: Example 2: In which phase of interphase is the DNA copied, and what happens to the amount of DNA?
examples.solution:
DNA replication happens in one specific sub-phase.

  • The S (synthesis) phase.
  • The amount of DNA doubles.
examples.answer: DNA is copied in the S phase, and the amount of DNA doubles.

examples.solution:
Some cells stop dividing.

  • G0 is an inactive (quiescent) stage outside the cycle.
  • Cells that no longer divide, such as mature nerve cells, enter it.
examples.answer: G0 is the quiescent (inactive) stage entered by cells that stop dividing, e.g. mature nerve cells.

recap:
• Cell cycle = orderly duplication and division of a cell (about 24 h in human cells).
  • Two stages: interphase (long) and M phase (short).
  • Interphase = G1 (growth), S (DNA replicates — doubles), G2 (growth, prepares to divide).
  • G0 = quiescent stage for non-dividing cells.

quiz.q: The DNA of a cell is copied during which phase?
quiz.explanation: DNA replication occurs in the S (synthesis) phase.

quiz.q: The long preparation stage of the cell cycle is called:
quiz.explanation: Interphase is the long preparatory stage before the M phase.

topics.title: Mitosis and Its Significance
topics.concept:
Mitosis is the division of the nucleus that produces two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell, each with the same number of chromosomes. It occurs in the body (somatic) cells and is therefore also called equational division. The nuclear division (karyokinesis) happens in four continuous stages:

  • Prophase — chromosomes condense and become visible (each as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere); the nuclear membrane and nucleolus begin to disappear; the spindle starts to form.
  • Metaphase — the chromosomes line up at the centre (equator) of the cell on the metaphase plate; spindle fibres attach to their centromeres.
  • Anaphase — the centromeres split and the sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell.
  • Telophase — chromosomes reach the poles and decondense; nuclear membranes re-form around each set, giving two nuclei.

After karyokinesis comes cytokinesis — the division of the cytoplasm. In animal cells a furrow pinches the cell in two; in plant cells a cell plate forms in the middle and grows outward into a new wall.

Significance of mitosis: it allows growth of the body, repair and replacement of worn-out cells (e.g. skin, blood), and keeps the chromosome number constant in all body cells. It is also the basis of asexual reproduction in many organisms.

examples.problem: Example 1: During which stage of mitosis do chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell?
examples.solution:
Recall the order of the stages.

  • Chromosomes align on the metaphase plate.
  • This happens in metaphase.

examples.problem: Example 2: How is cytokinesis different in plant and animal cells?
examples.solution:
The cytoplasm is divided differently.

  • Animal cells: a furrow pinches the cell into two.
  • Plant cells: a cell plate forms in the middle and grows into a new wall.
examples.answer: Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow; plant cells form a cell plate that grows into a new wall.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give two reasons why mitosis is important.
examples.solution:
Mitosis serves the body in several ways.

  • It allows growth of the organism.
  • It repairs and replaces worn-out cells, keeping the chromosome number constant.
examples.answer: Mitosis enables growth and the repair/replacement of cells while keeping the chromosome number constant.

recap:
• Mitosis = equational division giving 2 identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number; occurs in body cells.
  • Karyokinesis stages: prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase.
  • Cytokinesis: furrow (animals) or cell plate (plants).
  • Significance: growth, repair/replacement, constant chromosome number, asexual reproduction.

quiz.q: Mitosis produces daughter cells that are:
quiz.explanation: Mitosis is equational — daughter cells are identical with the same chromosome number.

quiz.q: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles during:
quiz.explanation: In anaphase the centromeres split and chromatids move to opposite poles.

topics.title: Meiosis, Crossing Over and Its Significance
topics.concept:
Meiosis is a special division that takes place in the reproductive cells and produces four daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number of the parent (haploid). It is therefore called reductional division. It involves two successive divisions — meiosis I and meiosis II — but the DNA is copied only once (before meiosis I).

Meiosis I is the reduction division. In its prophase I the homologous chromosomes (matching pairs, one from each parent) come together and pair up — a process called synapsis. While paired, they may exchange segments at points called chiasmata; this exchange is crossing over. Crossing over mixes the genes of the two parents, producing genetic recombination — new combinations of characters. The homologous chromosomes then separate to opposite poles, so each new cell gets only one of each pair (the chromosome number is halved).

Meiosis II is like mitosis: the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate, giving a total of four haploid cells.

Significance of meiosis: (1) it keeps the chromosome number constant from generation to generation — gametes are haploid, so when two fuse at fertilisation the normal (diploid) number is restored; and (2) crossing over and the random assortment of chromosomes create variation, which is the raw material for evolution.

examples.problem: Example 1: How many daughter cells does meiosis produce, and how does their chromosome number compare with the parent?
examples.solution:
Meiosis is reductional.

  • It produces four daughter cells.
  • Each has half the chromosome number of the parent (haploid).
examples.answer: Four daughter cells, each with half (haploid) the chromosome number of the parent.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is crossing over and why is it important?
examples.solution:
It happens during prophase I.

  • Crossing over is the exchange of segments between paired homologous chromosomes.
  • It mixes parental genes, producing genetic recombination (variation).
examples.answer: Crossing over is the exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes; it creates new gene combinations (variation).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why must gametes be formed by meiosis and not mitosis?
examples.solution:
Think about what happens at fertilisation.

  • Gametes must be haploid so that when two fuse, the normal diploid number is restored.
  • If gametes were made by mitosis, the chromosome number would double every generation.
examples.answer: So gametes are haploid; fertilisation then restores the normal diploid number and keeps it constant across generations.

recap:
• Meiosis = reductional division in reproductive cells; gives 4 haploid cells via two divisions (DNA copied once).
  • Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis), exchange segments (crossing over at chiasmata → recombination), then separate.
  • Meiosis II: sister chromatids separate (like mitosis).
  • Significance: keeps chromosome number constant across generations and creates variation for evolution.

quiz.q: Meiosis produces four daughter cells that are:
quiz.explanation: Meiosis is reductional — the four daughter cells are haploid.

quiz.q: The exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes is called:
quiz.explanation: Crossing over is the exchange of segments, producing genetic recombination.

questions.q: The orderly sequence by which a cell duplicates and divides is the:
questions.explanation: The cell cycle is the orderly sequence of duplication and division.

questions.q: The long preparation stage of the cell cycle is:
questions.explanation: Interphase is the long preparatory stage.

questions.q: DNA replication takes place during the:
questions.explanation: DNA is synthesised in the S phase.

questions.q: Cells that stop dividing, like mature nerve cells, enter the:
questions.explanation: Non-dividing cells enter the quiescent G0 stage.

questions.q: Division of the nucleus is called:
questions.explanation: Karyokinesis is nuclear division; cytokinesis is cytoplasmic division.

questions.q: Mitosis is also called:
questions.explanation: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same — equational division.

questions.q: Chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell during:
questions.explanation: In metaphase, chromosomes align on the metaphase plate.

questions.q: Sister chromatids separate to opposite poles during:
questions.explanation: Anaphase is when chromatids move to opposite poles.

questions.q: In plant cells, cytokinesis occurs by formation of a:
questions.explanation: Plant cells form a cell plate that grows into a new wall.

questions.q: Mitosis is important for all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number constant; meiosis halves it.

questions.q: Meiosis produces:
questions.explanation: Meiosis gives four haploid daughter cells.

questions.q: Meiosis is also known as:
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number — reductional division.

questions.q: Pairing of homologous chromosomes in prophase I is called:
questions.explanation: Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes.

questions.q: The exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes is:
questions.explanation: Crossing over exchanges segments and creates recombination.

questions.q: A key role of meiosis is to:
options: Double the chromosome number each generation
Keep the chromosome number constant across generations
questions.explanation: By making haploid gametes, meiosis keeps the number constant after fertilisation.

questions.q: If a cell has 16 chromosomes before the S phase, how many will it have at the end of the S phase?
questions.explanation: S phase doubles the DNA, not the chromosome number — 16 chromosomes, each now with two sister chromatids.

questions.q: A cell with 24 chromosomes undergoes mitosis. Each daughter cell will have:
questions.explanation: Mitosis is equational, so each daughter cell keeps 24 chromosomes.

questions.q: A cell with 24 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. Each of the four daughter cells will have:
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the number, so each haploid cell gets 12 chromosomes.

questions.q: Crossing over increases variation because it:
options: Produces new combinations of parental genes
questions.explanation: Exchanging segments between homologues creates new gene combinations — the basis of recombination.

questions.q: Why is meiosis II often compared to mitosis?
options: Sister chromatids separate, with no further reduction in number
questions.explanation: In meiosis II the sister chromatids separate (as in mitosis); the reduction already happened in meiosis I.

questions.q: If gametes were formed by mitosis instead of meiosis, over generations the chromosome number would:
questions.explanation: Diploid gametes fusing would double the number every generation; meiosis prevents this by making haploid gametes.
